headline: Dexory now sells perception accuracy as a contracted SLA per site, so the bottleneck is no longer collecting shelf scans but choosing which of the millions of near-identical frames to label and proving the Integrity models hold up site by site.
what_they_build: Dexory builds autonomous camera and sensor robots (now up to 18m AMRs) that drive warehouse aisles daily and feed DexoryView, a subscription platform that reconciles what the WMS says should be in a location against what is actually there. The Integrity module flags inventory discrepancies, damage and hygiene risks and rack compliance; Optimise handles slotting and space utilisation. Buyers are 3PL and enterprise logistics operators such as Iron Mountain, Ziegler, Romark and Stellantis sites.
inferred_pipeline: Robots run automated daily scan missions per aisle, capturing high-resolution imagery of every rack face plus (guess) LIDAR or depth for localisation and pallet geometry.
Scans are uploaded per site and per mission into cloud object storage, probably partitioned by customer, site, date and mission, with barcode or location-label reads tied to WMS slot IDs (guess).
Detection and OCR models produce occupancy, location ID and discrepancy outputs; newer Integrity classes (damage, hygiene, rack compliance) run on top of the same frames (guess).
Labelling is likely a mix of in-house tooling, an outsourced vendor and operations staff adjudicating flagged exceptions; we have no direct evidence of the tool used.
Model outputs are aggregated into per-site accuracy, scan coverage and obstruction metrics; the Founding Data Engineer ad says these are being modelled against committed SLAs and KPIs in Databricks.
Failures surface as customer-reported discrepancies, which (guess) are fed back manually as new training examples with no systematic way to find similar frames across sites.

hypotheses.pain: Massive redundancy: the same rack face is scanned daily, so labelling budget is spent on near-duplicate frames while rare damage and compliance events stay under-represented.
hypotheses.evidence: Daily automated scans across multi-site deployments (Iron Mountain expansion, Stellantis), plus new Integrity classes for damage, hygiene and rack compliance.
hypotheses.encord_answer: Index registers frames in their own bucket, computes embeddings and quality metrics, and lets them de-duplicate and diversity-sample into Collections. Our warehouse shelf-scan benchmark cut frames to label by 61% while keeping 95% of racks, and the curated pick beat a random pick of equal size.

hypotheses.pain: Perception accuracy is now a contractual SLA per site, but there is no systematic way to show where models fail by site, aisle, lighting or class.
hypotheses.evidence: Job ad: model perception accuracy, scan and mission performance, obstructions and scan coverage against SLAs and KPIs committed per site.
hypotheses.encord_answer: Active imports their predictions and reports mAP, F1, PR curves and confusion matrix sliced by class, IoU threshold and any data metric. Metric-to-failure correlation then tells them which frames to label next, feeding the per-site SLA story directly.

hypotheses.pain: New Integrity classes (damage, leaning pallets, hygiene risks) need fresh labels fast, and each new enterprise site brings new racking, lighting and pallet types that break the previous ontology.
hypotheses.evidence: Site text on Integrity module ML models; Storage Health launch Feb 2026; rapid multi-site expansion with Iron Mountain and Stellantis.
hypotheses.encord_answer: Annotate gives one ontology across images, native video and point clouds with SAM 3 auto-segmentation, tracking and interpolation, plus review workflows. Agents run their own detector as a pre-labelling stage so annotators correct rather than draw.

ontology.name: Pallet in location
ontology.why: Core occupancy signal reconciled against the WMS slot record

ontology.name: Empty or partially filled location
ontology.why: Drives inventory discrepancy and space utilisation outputs

ontology.name: Location or product barcode region
ontology.why: OCR region tying each detection to a WMS location ID

ontology.name: Damaged rack beam or upright
ontology.why: Rack compliance and safety flags need tight shape, not loose boxes

ontology.name: Leaning or overhanging pallet corners
ontology.why: Lean and overhang angle is geometric, keypoints measure it directly

ontology.name: Damaged or spilled stock, shrink wrap tear
ontology.why: Irregular damage extent for Integrity damage and hygiene risk

ontology.name: Aisle obstruction: debris, forklift, person
ontology.why: If LIDAR is used, obstruction and scan coverage metrics need 3D extent

ontology.name: Scan quality: motion blur, dark aisle, occluded face
ontology.why: Explains coverage gaps and filters frames before they reach annotators

case_study.name: Automotus, plus Encord's own warehouse shelf-scan benchmark
case_study.why_it_matches: Automotus runs fixed street cameras producing huge volumes of repetitive footage, the same redundancy problem as a daily rack scan. Our internal warehouse benchmark is closer still: public shelf images, three passes per rack, 10% degraded frames, exactly the shape of a Dexory mission.
case_study.numbers: Automotus: +20% mAP, 35% smaller dataset, 33% lower labelling cost after curating with Encord. Warehouse benchmark: 61% fewer frames to label keeping 95% of racks, YOLOv8n at 0.48 mAP50 curated versus 0.43 random at equal size.

proof_of_value: Week 1, day 1 to 2: register one site's scans from their existing S3 or Azure bucket into Index; no data movement, SOC2 Type II and GDPR in place. Success: embeddings and quality metrics on one week of missions from one site.

Week 1, day 3 to 5: de-duplicate near-identical rack passes and build a diversity Collection. Success metric: percentage reduction in candidate frames while retaining coverage of every rack face, target 50% or better.

Week 2, day 1 to 2: import their current Integrity model predictions into Active and slice performance by class, site, aisle and brightness or sharpness. Success: a named list of the three worst-performing slices tied to SLA risk.

Week 2, day 3 to 4: label the Active-recommended slice in Annotate with SAM 3 and an Agents pre-labelling stage using their own detector. Success: time per frame for damage polygons versus their current baseline.

Week 2, day 5: retrain or fine-tune on curated versus random picks of equal size and compare in Active. Success: measurable mAP or recall gain on damaged and leaning pallet classes, plus a cost-per-labelled-frame figure for the business case.
discovery_questions: How is perception accuracy defined and measured per site today, and who is accountable when a site drifts below the committed SLA?
When you launched the new Integrity classes for damage and rack compliance, how many frames did you label and how long did it take from decision to deployed model?
Of the frames a robot captures in a daily scan, roughly what fraction ever reaches an annotator, and how do you choose them?
What happens operationally when a customer disputes a discrepancy flag: does that frame get back into the training set, and can you find similar frames across other sites?
Can customer imagery from Iron Mountain or Stellantis sites leave your own cloud storage, and what does that rule out tool-wise?
risks: The visible hire is a Founding Data Engineer focused on business and SLA reporting in Databricks, not a perception data lead; our persona may not be hiring or budgeted right now.
Likely in-house annotation tooling built over several years alongside the robot stack, with sunk cost and an internal argument that shelf scans are simple enough to label cheaply offshore.
Enterprise customer imagery from logistics and automotive sites may carry contractual restrictions that slow any third-party tool through security review, even with data staying in their bucket.
Incumbent vendor or open-source stack (CVAT, Roboflow, a managed labelling BPO) already covers basic box labelling, so our wedge has to be curation and model evaluation, not labelling price.
